## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
There are no trials yet. The starting architecture scored 0.000 on both seeds. I read the starting code. The places-and-DONE action layout is (type, y, x) flattened, with DONE last, which matches concatenating per-type maps of shape [Y,X]. The observation has 4Z+3 channels. By my rough count, the baseline uses about 50k multiply-adds per cell, so a similar-sized network keeps r at about 1. The default recipe allows only about 32 updates of 4096 steps, which is very little for exact builds. Most likely, the zero comes from too few samples and a short reward horizon (gamma 0.95), not only from the architecture. For round 1, I'll test: (A) the baseline with a sample-rich recipe (1 epoch, gamma 0.99, lambda 0.95, ent 0.005); (B) a footprint-conv spatial head with normalised residual trunk, same recipe; (C) the same network with 2 epochs. This gives an architecture contrast (A vs B) and an epochs contrast (B vs C).

### Round 2
All four trials so far score 0 on dev and 0 on training success, across two heads and both 1 and 2 PPO epochs. So neither the number of samples nor the footprint head was the bottleneck. A likely cause: to score a placement, the network must find the brick's landing layer (the highest column height under its footprint) and check that every footprint cell is missing at exactly that layer. A 2D trunk that stacks all layers as channels has to learn that layer-matching comparison through a narrow per-cell MLP. My main bet is a shared per-layer network. Each layer z sees its own and neighbouring layers' current, target, missing and extra cells, the heights and a constant layer-index channel, so comparing height with z is easy to learn. A learned 3x3 head scores each brick type at each layer, and a logsumexp over layers gives one score per (type, cell). This is cheap 2D convolution batched over layers. A: lean version. B: adds a residual block. C: lean version with 2 epochs.

### Round 3
All six trials score 0 on both seeds, and none has any training success either. The architectures differed (pooled head, footprint conv, per-layer net), and so did the recipes (1 vs 2 epochs, more samples). The likely shared bottleneck is that exploration never finds an exact build, not a lack of capacity. The likeliest blocker is DONE. Early on, DONE is one action out of about 257. Placements earn positive shaping reward, so PPO quickly pushes DONE down everywhere. When a build is complete, DONE is almost never sampled, and the +1 bonus is never seen. A second concern is the anchor convention: footprint heads assume a top-left anchor and the world may differ, so a 3x3 head that does not assume an anchor is safer. Plan: put a learned factored DONE gate in every candidate (DONE logit = logsumexp of placement logits + learned d, so initially DONE has about the same probability as all placements combined). Then test it on the starting network, on a deeper generic residual network, and on that network with a longer-rollout recipe.

### Round 4
All nine trials scored exactly 0 on dev and 0 on training success, on both seeds. That covers the starting net, footprint-conv heads, per-layer nets, residual FCNs, 1 vs 2 PPO epochs, long rollouts and a DONE gate. The gated DONE starts near 50% per step, which probably ends episodes too early. Every failed net shared one assumption: that the action index runs in type-major, row-major, top-left-anchored order, so a conv output channel per type maps onto actions. The task says the world may differ from its description. If the env orders actions another way (transposed, or cell-major), every spatial head scores the wrong cells, and exact builds become nearly impossible. That would explain a uniform zero across varied architectures. This last round tests that idea with three heads that do not depend on the layout: a learned flat head, a hybrid of spatial and flat heads, and a learned mixture over plausible layouts. All keep the 1-epoch recipe with the most samples.
